disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Original puzzles written in the style of NSA's annual Codebreaker Challenge; not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the National Security Agency. No actual challenge content is reproduced — every puzzle here is original. Confers no certificate.

choices: It's random noise — no structure
It's a Caesar/rotation cipher — the flag format and letter patterns survive rotation; try all 25 shifts
It's AES — you'll need the key
It's Base64 — decode it directly
evidence: QODQ LV WKH IODJ LV JRRG OXFN
scenarios.hint: What happens to the letter pattern if you shift every letter back by the same amount?
scenarios.prompt: What kind of encoding is this, and how do you attack it?
scenarios.situation: You intercept a message. The word lengths and double letters look oddly familiar.
scenarios.title: The shifted message
scenarios.why: The preserved word structure and double letters scream monoalphabetic substitution — simplest case, a Caesar shift. With only 25 possible shifts, brute force is trivial: try each and look for English. Recognizing the cipher family from structure (before touching tools) is the core crypto-puzzle skill. (Shift back 3: 'FLAG IS THE FLAG IS GOOD LUCK' — well, you get the idea.)

choices: It's encrypted with a strong cipher — give up
XOR with a repeating key: the known header lets you recover keystream bytes and test the repetition
It's compressed — decompress it
It's a hash — irreversible
evidence: 1f0a1e0c0b... (bytes that XOR with 'FLAG{' reveal a repeating 4-byte pattern)
scenarios.hint: If you know the first five plaintext bytes, what does XORing them with the ciphertext give you?
scenarios.prompt: How do you recover the key?
scenarios.situation: A file is XOR-encrypted with a short repeating key. You know the plaintext starts with 'FLAG{'.
scenarios.title: Known plaintext, unknown key
scenarios.why: XOR's reversibility is its weakness: ciphertext XOR known-plaintext = keystream. Recover the first key bytes from the known header, then test whether the key repeats by decrypting further and checking for readable text. Known-plaintext attacks are the bread and butter of CTF crypto — always look for predictable headers, magic bytes, or format strings.

choices: Decode as Base64, then notice the result is hex, then decode the hex to ASCII
It's double-encrypted AES
It's a zip file — unzip it
The layers are a distraction; brute-force the original
evidence: 4e47566a... (long hex-looking string that itself decodes from Base64)
scenarios.hint: What does the character set tell you about the outermost layer?
scenarios.prompt: How do you unwrap this?
scenarios.situation: A blob's character set looks like Base64, but decoding gives something that looks like hex.
scenarios.title: Layers of encoding
scenarios.why: Encoding isn't encryption — it's just representation, and puzzles love stacking it. The character set identifies each layer: Base64 alphabet → decode; then hex digits → decode to bytes; then ASCII. Work outside-in, verifying each layer produces sensible output before proceeding. When a layer's output looks like another encoding, that's the next step, not a dead end.

choices: Try every password you can think of
Frequency analysis: count letter frequencies and map to English ETAOIN SHRDLU, using the flag format as an anchor
It's unbreakable without the key
Translate it as a different language
evidence: XMQ ZGNL... (long substitution-ciphered text, spaces preserved)
scenarios.hint: Which letter appears most — and what is the most common letter in English?
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic attack?
scenarios.situation: A long message is encrypted with a simple substitution cipher (each letter consistently replaced). Spaces are preserved.
scenarios.title: Counting letters
scenarios.why: Substitution preserves frequency: the most common ciphertext letter is probably E, and common short words and the flag format give anchors. Frequency analysis turns 'unbreakable-looking' text into a solvable puzzle — it's the oldest systematic cryptanalysis and still the right first move against classical ciphers. Length matters: more text, more reliable statistics.

choices: MD5 is broken so the hash is useless
Identify the hash type by length/format, then dictionary-attack with a targeted wordlist — weak passwords fall fast
Hashes can't be attacked
You need a quantum computer
scenarios.hint: What does 32 hex characters suggest — and what is the most likely plaintext for a puzzle?
scenarios.prompt: How do you approach this hash?
scenarios.situation: You recover a 32-character hex hash. You suspect it's a weak password.
scenarios.title: Name that hash
scenarios.why: 32 hex chars = 128 bits = MD5's signature. Against weak passwords, hashing is barely a speed bump: a dictionary attack with good wordlists (plus rules) cracks 'password'-class secrets in seconds. The lesson cuts both ways — puzzles teach why real systems need slow, salted password hashing. Identify by length, attack the password, not the algorithm.

choices: The key must be truly random and used once — a reused keystream lets you cancel the keys by XORing the two ciphertexts
One-time pads are unbreakable even with reuse
Use a longer key
Encrypt twice
scenarios.hint: What happens when you XOR the two ciphertexts together — where do the keys go?
scenarios.prompt: Both messages used a one-time pad. What's wrong?
scenarios.situation: Two messages were 'one-time-pad' encrypted, but traffic analysis suggests the same pad was used twice.
scenarios.title: The pad used twice
scenarios.why: A one-time pad is only unbreakable when the key is truly random, secret, and used ONCE. Reuse is catastrophic: C1 XOR C2 = P1 XOR P2, the keys cancel, and classic crib-dragging recovers both plaintexts. 'Never reuse the keystream' is the entire security of stream ciphers — puzzles love violating it, and real systems have fallen to the same mistake.

choices: Run it immediately to see what it does
Static first: run strings, check the file type, look at imports — understand it before executing anything untrusted
Delete it — analysis is too dangerous
Only run it on your main machine
evidence:
Enter the vault code:
Access granted. Welcome, operative.
Access denied.
SuperSecretCheck
scenarios.hint: What do the readable strings tell you about the program's logic — before you run a single instruction?
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe, productive first step?
scenarios.situation: You receive an unknown binary in a challenge. It's 64-bit ELF.
scenarios.title: Before you run it
scenarios.why: Strings reveal the program's vocabulary — prompts, success/failure messages, function names — which maps the logic without executing untrusted code. 'Enter the vault code' plus 'Access granted/denied' tells you it's a password check; SuperSecretCheck names the function to examine. Static-before-dynamic is the reversing discipline: understand, then execute (in a sandbox).

choices: The check is secure — assembly is hard to read

Read the comparison: if the code compares your input against the expected value byte-by-byte and early-exits, you can extract the expected value from the binary or brute-force per-character via timing
Assembly can't be analyzed
Just guess the password
evidence:
call SuperSecretCheck
test eax, eax
jz access_denied
scenarios.hint: Where must the correct answer exist for the program to check against it — and can you read that location?
scenarios.prompt: How do you defeat this check without guessing?
scenarios.situation: The binary checks a vault code. You have the disassembly showing a call to SuperSecretCheck.
scenarios.title: Reading the check
scenarios.why: The program must contain or derive the expected value to compare against — that value (or its construction) lives in the binary. Reversing the check function reveals whether the secret is embedded, transformed, or computed, and each case has an attack: extract it, replicate the transform, or attack the comparison itself. The check is the map to the secret.

choices: Patch the binary to always succeed — fastest
Understand the validation logic first, then decide: patching is legitimate in CTFs but understanding teaches the vuln class
Reversing is cheating
Only dynamic analysis is allowed
scenarios.hint: What do you learn from patching versus what do you learn from understanding?
scenarios.prompt: Is patching the binary to bypass the check acceptable?
scenarios.situation: You could NOP out the jump to 'access denied' and get the flag in seconds.
scenarios.title: The quick patch
scenarios.why: In CTFs, patching is a legitimate technique — but it's the end of learning, not the method. The challenge wants you to understand the validation logic (the vuln class, the crypto, the flaw); patching skips the lesson. Patch to confirm understanding, not to replace it. In real assessments, by contrast, you document the flaw — you don't patch the client's binary.

choices: It's packed/encrypted — give up
The input flows unsanitized into a dangerous sink (e.g., system/exec with format string); trace data flow from input to sink to find the injection
Input handling is always safe
Only the GUI matters
scenarios.hint: The validation checks one buffer — but which buffer actually overflows?
scenarios.prompt: Where is the vulnerability?
scenarios.situation: Decompilation shows input validation that looks correct at first glance.
scenarios.title: Follow the data
scenarios.why: The validation checks buf (64 bytes) but the overflow is in dest (32 bytes) — the check guards the wrong buffer. Reversing is data-flow analysis: trace untrusted input from source to every sink, and verify each check actually constrains the dangerous operation. 'Looks validated' is the most dangerous phrase in a binary; the data flow is the truth.

choices: Random guessing
Systematic: map inputs to behaviors, find the comparison or transformation, and attack the weakest link (embedded secret, weak transform, bypassable check)
Only experts can reverse
Use AI to write the flag
scenarios.hint: What are the three places the secret can live: in the binary, in the transform, or in the check?
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic methodology for an unknown binary challenge?
scenarios.situation: You're staring at a new reversing challenge with no hints.
scenarios.title: The method
scenarios.why: Reversing methodology: identify the file, extract strings, map the control flow around input handling, locate the validation/check, then classify the secret's location (embedded, transformed, or checked) and attack accordingly. Systematic beats brilliant — most challenge binaries fall to the methodical application of these steps, not to flashes of insight.

choices: Run it in an isolated sandbox/VM with snapshots, no network (or simulated network), and monitor its behavior — dynamic analysis complements static
Run it on your host — it's just a challenge
Never run unknown binaries under any circumstances
Dynamic analysis is obsolete
scenarios.hint: What does running it tell you that static analysis can't — and what must be true before you run it?
scenarios.prompt: When (and how) do you run the unknown binary?
scenarios.situation: Static analysis shows obfuscated logic you can't fully follow.
scenarios.title: Letting it run
scenarios.why: Dynamic analysis reveals runtime behavior — decrypted strings, actual control flow, network attempts — that static analysis can't. But it demands isolation: sandboxed VM, snapshots for reset, controlled/no network, and monitoring. The discipline is: static first to know what you're dealing with, dynamic to confirm, always contained. Curiosity without containment is how analysts become victims.

choices: It's normal — CDNs do that
Beaconing: regular intervals, consistent sizes, to an unusual domain — investigate the process and consider C2; verify against the host baseline
It's a software update — ignore it
Block the domain immediately with no investigation
evidence: 192.168.1.20 -> 203.0.113.9:443 every 60s, 184 bytes out, 96 bytes in, for 6 hours
scenarios.hint: What is regular about this — and what legitimate traffic is that regular?
scenarios.prompt: What does this pattern suggest?
scenarios.situation: A capture shows one internal host making perfectly regular HTTPS connections for hours.
scenarios.title: The metronome
scenarios.why: Metronomic timing with consistent byte counts to an unusual destination is the beaconing signature — automated check-ins, not human browsing. Humans are bursty and irregular; malware is punctual. Confirm with: domain age/reputation, whether the host should talk there, and jitter analysis. Then follow the stream — beacons often precede tasking.

choices: Read every packet — thoroughness matters
Filter and follow: isolate the suspicious stream (ip.addr/port), follow the TCP/UDP stream to reconstruct the conversation, then expand to the surrounding context
Only look at the first 100 packets
Captures that big are useless
scenarios.hint: What is the unit of meaning in a capture — the packet, or the conversation?
scenarios.prompt: How do you attack a 2 GB capture efficiently?
scenarios.situation: You're handed a 2 GB pcap and told 'the attack is in there.'
scenarios.title: Drinking from the firehose
scenarios.why: PCAP analysis is conversation-first: statistics and filters find the anomaly (unusual ports, large transfers, odd endpoints), then 'follow stream' reconstructs the meaningful exchange. Reading packet-by-packet is how analysts drown. The workflow — overview statistics, filter to interesting, follow streams, expand context — turns gigabytes into answers.

choices: DNS is always benign
Suspicious: internal host querying external DNS directly for odd domains, especially with TXT records or high entropy — possible tunneling/exfil; check the query patterns and the resolver
It's just misconfigured — ignore it
Block port 53 network-wide
evidence:
a1b2c3.query.example-dns.net TXT
f7e8d9.query.example-dns.net TXT ... (hundreds, unique subdomains)
scenarios.hint: What can a TXT record carry — and why would subdomains need to be unique?
scenarios.prompt: What is suspicious here?
scenarios.situation: The capture shows DNS TXT queries with unique high-entropy subdomains to an unknown domain.
scenarios.title: DNS tells stories
scenarios.why: TXT records can carry arbitrary data, and unique high-entropy subdomains are how tunneled data gets encoded upstream. Direct-to-external DNS bypasses monitored resolvers. In the capture, check: query volume vs baseline, response sizes (data coming back down?), and which process owns it. DNS is the attacker's favorite covert channel precisely because defenders under-monitor it.

choices: Certificate errors are normal
The handshake anomalies (odd cipher, self-signed, or JA3 mismatch) plus the destination suggest encrypted C2 — investigate the endpoint and process; TLS hides content, not metadata
Encrypted traffic can't be analyzed
Block all TLS
scenarios.hint: What does TLS hide — and what does it leave visible?
scenarios.prompt: How do you analyze suspicious encrypted traffic?
scenarios.situation: A host makes TLS connections to an IP with no hostname, using an unusual cipher suite.
scenarios.title: Reading the envelope
scenarios.why: TLS hides content but leaks metadata: destination, timing, byte counts, handshake parameters (SNI, ciphers, certificates, JA3 fingerprints). Analysts work the envelope — fingerprint the client, check cert anomalies, correlate timing with host activity. 'It's encrypted' ends content analysis; metadata analysis is where the answers live.

choices: Large transfers are normal
Scope the transfer: what host, what destination, what protocol, what time — then determine if it's authorized (baseline) or exfiltration; check for encryption/obfuscation
Immediately disconnect the host
It's just a backup
scenarios.hint: What distinguishes a backup from exfiltration — the bytes, or the context?
scenarios.prompt: How do you assess this?
scenarios.situation: The capture shows a 4 GB outbound transfer at 3 AM from a workstation to an external IP.
scenarios.title: Four gigabytes at 3 AM
scenarios.why: Bytes don't speak; context does. The assessment: is this host supposed to send data there (baseline)? Is the destination reputable? Does the timing/protocol match legitimate use (backup window, sanctioned tool)? Workstations pushing gigabytes to unknown externals at 3 AM is exfil until proven backup. Verify before you accuse — but investigate before you dismiss.

choices: ARP is layer 2 — not in scope
The capture shows duplicate ARP replies / gratuitous ARP from an unexpected MAC claiming the gateway — possible ARP spoofing; verify the legitimate MAC and investigate the claiming host
ARP traffic is always benign
It's a switch misconfiguration — ignore
evidence:
Who has 192.168.1.1? Tell 192.168.1.50
Reply 192.168.1.1 is-at aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff (unexpected MAC, repeated)
scenarios.hint: Who should be answering for the gateway — and who actually is?
scenarios.prompt: What does this ARP traffic indicate?
scenarios.situation: The capture shows rapid ARP replies for the gateway IP from a MAC that isn't the gateway's.
scenarios.title: Who's the gateway?
scenarios.why: Unsolicited, repeated ARP replies claiming the gateway IP from a non-gateway MAC is ARP spoofing — positioning for man-in-the-middle. Confirm by checking the gateway's real MAC (from a trusted source), then investigate the claiming host. In a challenge, this is often the pivot to intercepting credentials; in reality, it's the LAN attack every flat network enables.

choices: Nothing — deleted is deleted
Carve for file signatures: search the image for magic bytes (e.g., PNG, ZIP headers), extract candidate files, and validate them — deleted files' data often survives
Only the filename can be recovered
Reinstall the OS and the files come back
evidence: Disk image, 20 GB. User deleted 'secret.png' yesterday. Filesystem metadata is partially overwritten.
scenarios.hint: What does every file format start with — and does deleting update those bytes?
scenarios.prompt: How do you recover the deleted image?
scenarios.situation: A disk image contains a deleted PNG. Filesystem metadata is damaged.
scenarios.title: Carving the disk
scenarios.why: File carving ignores the filesystem and scans raw bytes for magic numbers (PNG's 89 50 4E 47...), then extracts until the footer. Deletion usually unlinks metadata without wiping content — the bytes persist until overwritten. Validate carved files (do they parse as PNG?) because carving produces false positives. It's the forensics answer to 'deleted.'

choices: The file's modified date is the truth
Build a timeline: combine filesystem timestamps, log entries, and application artifacts — corroborate across sources, and treat any single timestamp as untrusted (timestomping exists)
Only creation dates matter
Timestamps can't be faked
evidence: session for the suspect user at 2026-10-02 22:14
scenarios.hint: Which timestamp did the attacker set — and which sources didn't they touch?
scenarios.prompt: How do you establish when the file really appeared?
scenarios.situation: A malware file claims a 2020 date, but logs show the suspect active last week.
scenarios.title: When was it really?
scenarios.why: Timestomping fakes filesystem timestamps, but attackers rarely fake everything: log entries, prefetch, registry keys, and network flows corroborate the real timeline. Forensic time analysis is correlation — the round-number 2020 date is itself evidence of tampering. One timestamp is a claim; a corroborated timeline is a finding.

choices: Metadata is just trivia
Extract EXIF/metadata: camera, timestamps, GPS, software tags — then verify consistency (does the GPS match the story? do timestamps align?) — metadata lies when it's planted, so corroborate
Metadata is always accurate
Only the image pixels matter
evidence: CreateDate: 2026:10:03, GPS: (coordinates in the ocean), Software: Photoshop
scenarios.hint: What does each metadata field claim — and do the claims agree with each other?
scenarios.prompt: What does the metadata tell you, and how far do you trust it?
scenarios.situation: An image is evidence in your challenge scenario. Its metadata is... interesting.
scenarios.title: Reading the metadata
scenarios.why: Metadata is claims about the file — useful, but planted metadata is a classic misdirection. The analysis: extract everything (timestamps, GPS, software), check internal consistency (ocean GPS + 'photo of downtown' = lie), and corroborate externally. Metadata analysis is as much about spotting the forgery as reading the fields.

choices: Search for the keyword once and stop
String-search the image for indicators (IPs, URLs, flag formats), then examine hits in context — strings find what structure misses
Strings are obsolete
Only search for 'flag'
scenarios.hint: What survives deletion, encryption-failure, and filesystem damage — the raw bytes?
scenarios.prompt: What is the role of string searching in forensics?
scenarios.situation: You have a memory image and a disk image, and no idea where the evidence is.
scenarios.title: Strings as sonar
scenarios.why: Strings are the wide-area search: IPs, domains, email addresses, flag formats, and error messages survive in raw bytes long after structure is gone. Search broadly, then examine each hit's context (what surrounds it? which process? what offset?). It's triage, not conclusion — strings find candidates; analysis confirms them.

choices: Wipe it and move on
Memory forensics: analyze the memory image for running processes, network connections, injected code, and encryption keys — volatile evidence dies at shutdown
Memory only matters for Windows
Reboot and check the disk
scenarios.hint: What exists only in memory — never touching disk?
scenarios.prompt: The disk looks clean but the machine was acting strangely while running. What's next?
scenarios.situation: You have a memory capture from the suspect machine taken before shutdown.
scenarios.title: What the disk doesn't know
scenarios.why: Fileless malware, injected code, active network connections, and decryption keys live only in memory — the disk can be pristine while the machine is owned. Memory analysis (process lists, connection tables, code injection artifacts) catches what disk forensics misses. The capture-before-shutdown discipline is what makes this possible; after reboot, it's gone.

choices: Document everything: what you collected, when, how, hashes of images, and who handled them — analyze copies, never originals
Just start analyzing — documentation slows you down
Chain of custody is only for law enforcement
Hashes are optional
scenarios.hint: Six months from now, how do you prove the evidence is unchanged since collection?
scenarios.prompt: What makes your forensic findings defensible?
scenarios.situation: Your challenge solution might be reviewed — or your real investigation might go to HR/legal.
scenarios.title: Defensible forensics
scenarios.why: Findings rest on handling: cryptographic hashes prove images are unchanged, contemporaneous notes prove your process, and access records prove custody. Analyze copies so the original stays pristine. This discipline separates forensics from tinkering — and it's what lets your conclusions survive skeptical review.

choices: It's just an error message
Error-based information disclosure: the errors reveal stack traces/queries — map the tech stack from them, then test the injection properly with safe proofs
Errors mean the app is broken, not vulnerable
Only report it if you get a shell
evidence: SQLSTATE[HY000]: syntax error near '' OR '1'='1' at line 1 ... MySQL ...
scenarios.hint: What did the error just tell you — the database type, the query structure, or both?
scenarios.prompt: What do you learn from this error, and what's next?
scenarios.situation: A search field returns verbose database errors when you enter a quote.
scenarios.title: The talkative error
scenarios.why: Verbose errors are reconnaissance gold: database type, query structure, sometimes table names — everything needed to craft a precise injection. The methodology: let errors map the backend, then prove injection with minimal safe tests (boolean/time-based), and recommend generic error handling plus parameterized queries. The error didn't create the vuln; it advertised it.

choices: It's a feature — users share links
Broken access control: the server trusts the client-supplied ID without an ownership check — verify methodically and minimally, then report with the authorization fix
It's fine if the IDs are hard to guess
Only test your own account
scenarios.hint: Who authorized you to see document 9917 — you, or nobody?
scenarios.prompt: What is the flaw, and how do you test it responsibly?
scenarios.situation: Incrementing a document ID shows other users' documents.
scenarios.title: Someone else's document
scenarios.why: The server never checks ownership — IDOR, the most common serious web flaw. Responsible testing: confirm with minimal access (view, don't modify/exfiltrate), document the pattern, and recommend server-side authorization checks on every object reference. 'Hard to guess IDs' is not a fix; authorization is.

choices: Client-side validation is sufficient
The client is attacker-controlled: move all validation and authorization server-side, and treat anything from the client as untrusted input
It's fine for low-risk apps
Only validate the price field
scenarios.hint: What stops an attacker from just... not running your JavaScript?
scenarios.prompt: What is the fundamental flaw?
scenarios.situation: The admin panel is 'hidden' by JavaScript, but the API endpoints respond without any server-side role check.
scenarios.title: Hidden is not secured
scenarios.why: Client-side controls are UI conveniences, not security: attackers proxy around them in seconds. Every authorization decision must be enforced server-side, on every request. The hidden panel is the classic demo — the API behind it is the actual vulnerability. Never trust the client; it belongs to the attacker.

choices: Test the session lifecycle: predictable tokens, no expiry, no invalidation on logout/password change — each is a takeover vector; recommend random, expiring, properly-invalidated sessions
Sessions are the framework's problem
Long sessions are user-friendly and fine
Only test over HTTPS
evidence: sessionid=10042 (sequential); still valid 30 days after logout
scenarios.hint: What should happen to a session at logout — and what does 'still valid' mean for an attacker with the cookie?
scenarios.prompt: What session flaws do you test for?
scenarios.situation: Session IDs are sequential and survive logout.
scenarios.title: The immortal session
scenarios.why: Session testing covers the lifecycle: unpredictability (random, not sequential), expiry (absolute and idle), and invalidation (logout and password change must kill sessions). A post-logout-valid session means 'logout' is theater — stolen cookies work forever. Each lifecycle gap is an account-takeover path; test them all systematically.

choices: Fuzz randomly — volume finds bugs
Methodical: map the input surface, test each input's type/length/encoding assumptions, observe error and behavior differences, then focus where the app 'thinks' differently than you do
Only fuzz login forms
Fuzzing is too noisy for challenges
scenarios.hint: What are you actually looking for — crashes, or the app's assumptions breaking?
scenarios.prompt: What is the disciplined approach to input testing?
scenarios.situation: A challenge app has dozens of inputs and you have limited time.
scenarios.title: Fuzzing with a brain
scenarios.why: Effective input testing is hypothesis-driven: enumerate inputs, note each one's apparent expectations, then violate them deliberately (types, lengths, encodings, special characters) and watch for differential behavior — errors, timing changes, reflections. Random fuzzing finds crashes; methodical fuzzing finds logic flaws. Prioritize inputs that reach dangerous sinks (queries, commands, file paths).

choices: It's low risk — it just fetches a URL
SSRF: the server fetches attacker-chosen URLs — probe safely (can it reach internal/metadata addresses?), demonstrate minimally, and recommend strict allowlisting of fetch targets
It's an open redirect
Only exploitable by admins
scenarios.hint: Whose network position is the request coming from — yours, or the server's?
scenarios.prompt: What is the vulnerability and the key risk?
scenarios.situation: A URL-preview feature fetches arbitrary URLs, including cloud metadata addresses.
scenarios.title: The server fetches for you
scenarios.why: SSRF weaponizes the server's network position: it can reach internal services and cloud metadata endpoints that you can't. The metadata service is the classic target — instance credentials. Demonstrate with minimal safe requests (reachability, not credential theft), and fix with allowlists plus network-level blocks on metadata addresses. The feature's helpfulness is the vulnerability.

choices: Write the whole solver at once — faster
Decompose: parse the format, implement the transform, test on the given example, then run on the challenge input — verify each stage
Solvers don't need testing
Copy a solver from the internet
scenarios.hint: What is the smallest piece you can verify before building the rest?
scenarios.prompt: What is the disciplined way to write a challenge solver?
scenarios.situation: A programming challenge gives you a custom-encoded file and one worked example.
scenarios.title: Building the solver
scenarios.why: Solver discipline mirrors software discipline: parse, transform, verify against the example, then execute on the real input. The worked example is your test case — if the solver can't reproduce it, the solver is wrong. Debugging a monolithic untested solver wastes hours; staged verification catches errors where they're born.

choices: Guess the flag format
Read the spec: implement exactly what it describes, handle the edge cases it names, and test against its examples — specs are the challenge's contract
Specs are misleading — ignore them
Only the examples matter
scenarios.hint: What did the challenge author promise — and what did they warn about?
scenarios.prompt: A binary-format challenge ships a 3-page spec. How do you use it?
scenarios.situation: The spec describes a custom file format with edge cases and two examples.
scenarios.title: Read the manual
scenarios.why: The spec is the challenge's contract: it tells you exactly what to implement, including the edge cases that distinguish solvers that work from solvers that almost work. Implement to the spec, test against its examples, and handle its named edge cases. Skipping the spec is how you burn hours on a misread format.

choices: Brute-force the entire keyspace — computers are fast
Bound the problem: use the challenge's constraints (key length hints, known plaintext, format) to shrink the search, then automate the reduced space
Brute force never works
Give up if it's more than 4 characters
scenarios.hint: What do you actually know — and how much does each known fact shrink the search?
scenarios.prompt: When is brute force the right tool?
scenarios.situation: A challenge hints at a 4-character lowercase key for a simple cipher.
scenarios.title: Smart brute force
scenarios.why: Brute force is legitimate when the space is bounded: 26^4 is ~456k — trivial. The skill is bounding: use every constraint (character set, length, known plaintext, format checks) to shrink the space before automating, and build in early verification (does the output look right?). Dumb brute force of huge spaces wastes time; bounded brute force with verification is a precision tool.

choices: Eyeball the hexdump
Script it: parse the structure programmatically, extract the fields, and let the computer do the repetitive work — humans spot patterns, scripts apply them
Manual analysis is more reliable
Only use GUI tools
scenarios.hint: What is the computer better at than you — and what are you better at?
scenarios.prompt: You must extract 500 records from a custom binary format. How?
scenarios.situation: Hand-decoding one record took 20 minutes. There are 500.
scenarios.title: Script the boring parts
scenarios.why: The division of labor: humans recognize the pattern once, scripts apply it 500 times without transcription errors. Write the parser, verify it on the hand-decoded record, then run it on all 500. 'I'll just do them by hand' is how challenges eat your weekend — and how real analysts burn out on repetitive triage.

choices: Reimplement the described algorithm exactly and test against known vectors before touching the challenge data
Write it from memory — you know crypto
Skip testing — the challenge input is the test
Use a library that does something similar
scenarios.hint: How do you know your implementation is right — before it matters?
scenarios.prompt: A challenge requires implementing a described cipher. What's the safe approach?
scenarios.situation: The challenge describes a custom Feistel-like cipher with a test vector.
scenarios.title: Implementing the cipher
scenarios.why: Crypto implementation bugs are silent: the code runs, the output looks plausible, and it's wrong. Test vectors are the antidote — implement, then verify byte-for-byte against the given vector before touching challenge data. One wrong rotation or endianness choice poisons everything downstream; vectors catch it in seconds. This mirrors real crypto engineering discipline.

choices: Optimize first — speed matters
Correct first, then fast: get a working solver, verify on examples, then optimize only the bottleneck with profiling — premature optimization breaks solvers
Slow solvers never finish
Optimization is cheating
scenarios.hint: What is slower: a slow solver, or a fast solver that's wrong?
scenarios.prompt: Your solver works but is slow on the full input. What now?
scenarios.situation: The solver cracks the example in seconds but will take hours on the real data.
scenarios.title: Slow but right
scenarios.why: A correct slow solver beats a fast wrong one — always. Profile to find the actual bottleneck (it's never where you guess), optimize that, and re-verify against the example after every change. Most 'slow solver' problems are algorithmic (wrong approach) not constant-factor; but you only discover that by measuring, not guessing.

lessons.title: Crypto Puzzles — Core concepts
concepts: Classical ciphers: frequency analysis turns 'unbreakable-looking' text into a solvable puzzle — it's the oldest systematic cryptanalysis and still the right first move against classical ciphers.
XOR's reversibility is its weakness: ciphertext XOR known-plaintext = keystream. Reuse is catastrophic: C1 XOR C2 = P1 XOR P2, the keys cancel, and classic crib-dragging recovers both plaintexts.

Known-plaintext attacks are the bread and butter of CTF crypto — always look for predictable headers, magic bytes, or format strings. Against weak passwords, hashing is barely a speed bump: a dictionary attack with good wordlists (plus rules) cracks 'password'-class secrets in seconds.
Encoding isn't encryption — it's just representation, and puzzles love stacking it.
Character set analysis: the character set identifies each layer: Base64 alphabet → decode; then hex digits → decode to bytes; then ASCII.

example.code: 1f0a1e0c0b... (bytes that XOR with 'FLAG{' reveal a repeating 4-byte pattern)
example.walkthrough: XOR's reversibility is its weakness: ciphertext XOR known-plaintext = keystream. Recover the first key bytes from the known header, then test whether the key repeats by decrypting further and checking for readable text.

pitfalls: Common trap: one-time pads are unbreakable even with reuse.
Common trap: the layers are a distraction; brute-force the original.
Common trap: MD5 is broken so the hash is useless.
Common trap: try every password you can think of.

lessons.title: Reverse Engineering — Core concepts
concepts: Static analysis: dynamic analysis reveals runtime behavior — decrypted strings, actual control flow, network attempts — that static analysis can't. Reversing is data-flow analysis: trace untrusted input from source to every sink, and verify each check actually constrains the dangerous operation.

Strings: reversing methodology: identify the file, extract strings, map the control flow around input handling, locate the validation/check, then classify the secret's location (embedded, transformed, or checked) and attack accordingly.
Reverse engineering logic: the challenge wants you to understand the validation logic (the vuln class, the crypto, the flaw); patching skips the lesson.
Static extraction: the discipline is: static first to know what you're dealing with, dynamic to confirm, always contained.
Patching: in CTFs, patching is a legitimate technique — but it's the end of learning, not the method.

example.code:
call SuperSecretCheck
test eax, eax
jz access_denied
example.walkthrough: The program must contain or derive the expected value to compare against — that value (or its construction) lives in the binary. Reversing the check function reveals whether the secret is embedded, transformed, or computed, and each case has an attack: extract it, replicate the transform, or attack the comparison itself. The check is the map to the secret.

pitfalls: Common trap: never run unknown binaries under any circumstances.
Skipping the key question: what do the readable strings tell you about the program's logic — before you run a single instruction.
Skipping the key question: where must the correct answer exist for the program to check against it — and can you read that location.

lessons.title: Network Analysis — Core concepts
concepts: Beaconing detection: metronomic timing with consistent byte counts to an unusual destination is the beaconing signature — automated check-ins, not human browsing.
PCAP analysis is conversation-first: statistics and filters find the anomaly (unusual ports, large transfers, odd endpoints), then 'follow stream' reconstructs the meaningful exchange.
Stream analysis: 'It's encrypted' ends content analysis; metadata analysis is where the answers live. Then follow the stream — beacons often precede tasking.
DNS forensics: direct-to-external DNS bypasses monitored resolvers.

example.code:
a1b2c3.query.example-dns.net TXT
f7e8d9.query.example-dns.net TXT ... (hundreds, unique subdomains)
example.walkthrough: TXT records can carry arbitrary data, and unique high-entropy subdomains are how tunneled data gets encoded upstream. In the capture, check: query volume vs baseline, response sizes (data coming back down?), and which process owns it. DNS is the attacker's favorite covert channel precisely because defenders under-monitor it.

pitfalls: Common trap: block the domain immediately with no investigation.
Skipping the key question: what is regular about this — and what legitimate traffic is that regular.
Skipping the key question: what is the unit of meaning in a capture — the packet, or the conversation.

lessons.title: Forensics — Core concepts
concepts: File carving ignores the filesystem and scans raw bytes for magic numbers (PNG's 89 50 4E 47...), then extracts until the footer. Metadata is claims about the file — useful, but planted metadata is a classic misdirection.

Magic bytes: deletion usually unlinks metadata without wiping content — the bytes persist until overwritten. Strings are the wide-area search: IPs, domains, email addresses, flag formats, and error messages survive in raw bytes long after structure is gone.

Timeline analysis: memory analysis (process lists, connection tables, code injection artifacts) catches what disk forensics misses. Forensic time analysis is correlation — the round-number 2020 date is itself evidence of tampering.
Timestomping fakes filesystem timestamps, but attackers rarely fake everything: log entries, prefetch, registry keys, and network flows corroborate the real timeline.
Metadata analysis is as much about spotting the forgery as reading the fields. It's triage, not conclusion — strings find candidates; analysis confirms them.

example.code: Disk image, 20 GB. User deleted 'secret.png' yesterday. Filesystem metadata is partially overwritten.
example.walkthrough: File carving ignores the filesystem and scans raw bytes for magic numbers (PNG's 89 50 4E 47...), then extracts until the footer. Validate carved files (do they parse as PNG?) because carving produces false positives. It's the forensics answer to 'deleted.'.

pitfalls: Common trap: chain of custody is only for law enforcement.
Common trap: the file's modified date is the truth.
Common trap: reinstall the OS and the files come back.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Web Exploitation — Core concepts
concepts: Error handling: the methodology: let errors map the backend, then prove injection with minimal safe tests (boolean/time-based), and recommend generic error handling plus parameterized queries.
IDOR: the server never checks ownership — IDOR, the most common serious web flaw.

Authorization testing: responsible testing: confirm with minimal access (view, don't modify/exfiltrate), document the pattern, and recommend server-side authorization checks on every object reference.
Client-side controls are UI conveniences, not security: attackers proxy around them in seconds.
Server-side validation: every authorization decision must be enforced server-side, on every request.

example.code: SQLSTATE[HY000]: syntax error near '' OR '1'='1' at line 1 ... MySQL ...
example.walkthrough: Verbose errors are reconnaissance gold: database type, query structure, sometimes table names — everything needed to craft a precise injection. The error didn't create the vuln; it advertised it.

pitfalls: Common trap: errors mean the app is broken, not vulnerable.
Common trap: it's fine if the IDs are hard to guess.
Common trap: long sessions are user-friendly and fine.

lessons.title: Programming Challenges — Core concepts
concepts: Solver development: the worked example is your test case — if the solver can't reproduce it, the solver is wrong. A correct slow solver beats a fast wrong one — always.

Verification: dumb brute force of huge spaces wastes time; bounded brute force with verification is a precision tool. Debugging a monolithic untested solver wastes hours; staged verification catches errors where they're born.
Edge cases: the spec is the challenge's contract: it tells you exactly what to implement, including the edge cases that distinguish solvers that work from solvers that almost work.
Search space reduction: brute force is legitimate when the space is bounded: 26^4 is ~456k — trivial.

lessons.title: Codebreaker-Style Challenges — Core concepts
concepts: Ciphers, encodings, and hashes are different tools: ciphers hide meaning with a key, encodings just change representation, and hashes are one-way fingerprints. Confusing them causes real breaches.
Classical ciphers fall to statistics: monoalphabetic substitutions preserve letter frequencies, and tiny keyspaces (25 Caesar shifts, 256 XOR bytes) fall to brute force in milliseconds.
Identify before you attack: hash length fingerprints the algorithm (32 hex chars = MD5, 64 = SHA-256), magic bytes reveal true file types, and Base64's alphabet gives it away instantly.
Forensics starts with the bytes, not the label: extensions lie, magic numbers don't — verify format with file-type signatures before trusting or executing anything.
Reverse engineering begins with the easy wins: 'strings', file-type identification, and hex inspection surface hardcoded secrets and hidden functionality before you ever open a disassembler.

example.walkthrough: Piping a suspicious blob through base64 -d instantly tests the encoding hypothesis — if readable text comes out, you have identified obfuscation, not encryption. Build this reflex: decode first, then decide whether real cryptography is even involved.

pitfalls: Common trap: calling Base64 'encryption' — it is encoding, keyless and instantly reversible.
Common trap: trusting file extensions — verify with magic bytes via the 'file' command or a hex viewer.
Common trap: assuming a hash is secure storage — unsalted fast hashes (MD5, SHA-1) are built for speed, which is exactly what attackers want.
Common trap: hiding secrets with obfuscation instead of moving them to a vault — strings, decompilers, and debuggers see through it.

simulations.brief: A captured message decodes to gibberish under ROT13 but the briefing says it is a simple substitution. Work it through.

evidence: Wkh txlfn eurzq ira mxpsv ryhu wkh odcb grj
The message uses a simple substitution cipher.
steps.explain: ROT13 is one specific shift; a general substitution needs frequency analysis, not a single fixed shift. The gibberish proves the assumption wrong.
options: ROT13 failed, so try frequency analysis for a general substitution
Assume the message is random noise
steps.symptom: ROT13 produces gibberish on a 'simple substitution' message.

evidence: Most common letter in the message: K. In English: E.

options: Map K to E and decode the rest from context
Map K to Z for variety

evidence: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog

PCAP analysis is conversation-first — statistics and filters find the anomaly (unusual ports, large transfers, odd endpoints), then 'follow stream' reconstructs the meaningful exchange.
Stream analysis — 'It's encrypted' ends content analysis; metadata analysis is where the answers live. Then follow the stream — beacons often precede tasking.
DNS forensics — direct-to-external DNS bypasses monitored resolvers.
Common trap — block the domain immediately with no investigation.

sections.heading: Forensics
items: File — File carving ignores the filesystem and scans raw bytes for magic numbers (PNG's 89 50 4E 47...), then extracts until the footer. Metadata is claims about the file — useful, but planted metadata is a classic misdirection.

Magic bytes — deletion usually unlinks metadata without wiping content — the bytes persist until overwritten. Strings are the wide-area search: IPs, domains, email addresses, flag formats, and error messages survive in raw bytes long after structure is gone.

Timeline analysis — memory analysis (process lists, connection tables, code injection artifacts) catches what disk forensics misses. Forensic time analysis is correlation — the round-number 2020 date is itself evidence of tampering.
Timestomping — Timestomping fakes filesystem timestamps, but attackers rarely fake everything: log entries, prefetch, registry keys, and network flows corroborate the real timeline.
Metadata analysis — is as much about spotting the forgery as reading the fields. It's triage, not conclusion — strings find candidates; analysis confirms them.
Common trap — chain of custody is only for law enforcement.
Common trap — the file's modified date is the truth.
Common trap — reinstall the OS and the files come back.

sections.heading: Web Exploitation
items: Error handling — the methodology: let errors map the backend, then prove injection with minimal safe tests (boolean/time-based), and recommend generic error handling plus parameterized queries.
IDOR — the server never checks ownership — IDOR, the most common serious web flaw.

Authorization testing — responsible testing: confirm with minimal access (view, don't modify/exfiltrate), document the pattern, and recommend server-side authorization checks on every object reference.
Client-side controls are UI conveniences, not security — attackers proxy around them in seconds.
Server-side validation — every authorization decision must be enforced server-side, on every request.
Common trap — errors mean the app is broken, not vulnerable.
Common trap — it's fine if the IDs are hard to guess.
Common trap — long sessions are user-friendly and fine.
Verbose errors are reconnaissance gold — database type, query structure, sometimes table names — everything needed to craft a precise injection. The error didn't create the vuln; it advertised it.

sections.heading: Programming Challenges
items: Solver development — the worked example is your test case — if the solver can't reproduce it, the solver is wrong. A correct slow solver beats a fast wrong one — always.

Verification — dumb brute force of huge spaces wastes time; bounded brute force with verification is a precision tool. Debugging a monolithic untested solver wastes hours; staged verification catches errors where they're born.
Edge cases — the spec is the challenge's contract: it tells you exactly what to implement, including the edge cases that distinguish solvers that work from solvers that almost work.
Search space reduction — brute force is legitimate when the space is bounded: 26^4 is ~456k — trivial.
Common trap — use a library that does something similar.
Skipping the key question — what is the smallest piece you can verify before building the rest.
Skipping the key question — what did the challenge author promise — and what did they warn about.

Read — Read the setup and name the principle at play before looking at the reasoning. Then compare your answer with the takeaway — if they differ, re-read the concepts above and try the drill scenarios for this domain.

glossary.def: XOR's reversibility is its weakness: ciphertext XOR known-plaintext = keystream. Reuse is catastrophic: C1 XOR C2 = P1 XOR P2, the keys cancel, and classic crib-dragging recovers both plaintexts.

checklist: Sleep 7–8 hours — puzzle speed collapses under fatigue.
Set up your workspace: notes app, scratch paper, and the bootcamp terminal ready.
Read each challenge prompt fully before touching the keyboard.
Work methodically: enumerate possibilities before guessing.
When stuck for 15 minutes, switch challenges and return with fresh eyes.
Document every solved technique in your own words — it compounds.
Time-box each challenge; bank the easy wins first.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
Replay the Crypto Puzzles challenges until your solve time drops.
Write up your Reverse Engineering solutions as if teaching a teammate.
Replay the Network Analysis challenges until your solve time drops.
